a_consequence_stated_rather_than_discove: An open pull request now carries NO required checks until a nightly run reports them, so it sits unmergeable all day and GitHub shows its status as blocked. That is the intended state of a delivery candidate under this model, not a stuck pull request, and it is written into the gate workflows themselves so the next person to look does not treat it as a fault.
two_validators_contradicted_each_other:
Removing the trigger made tools/project-state.py fail with 'governance CI must run on pull_request', while tools/validate-delivery-protocol.py refuses exactly that trigger. Two validators asserting opposite things about the same line is worse than either being wrong, because whichever one is edited to agree looks like the other was right.

Resolved by locating the question in ONE place. project-state.py keeps everything it was actually protecting -- the gate exists, targets master, runs every required command, ignores no failure, asserts a clean tree -- and now requires the nightly workflow_dispatch instead of pull_request. WHICH EVENT earns a required context is asserted only by validate-delivery-protocol.py, against the model the register declares.
the_regression_this_delivery_exists_to_p:
M61f reintroduces a pull_request trigger on a gate -- the daytime interruption, back -- and the suite requires it to be detected.

ITS FIRST ANCHOR WAS WRONG AND THE PROOF SILENTLY PASSED, which is worth recording because it is the fifth instance of the same family in this mission. The anchor was 'on:\n  push:', which no longer exists: removing pull_request left a long comment between 'on:' and 'push:'. So the mutation replaced nothing, the validator correctly reported PASS on an unmutated file, and the run looked like evidence of detection. A mutation whose anchor does not resolve proves the opposite of what it appears to. The anchor now targets the push block, which exists, and the refusal names the model.

the_model_caught_a_defect_in_its_own_act:
THE FIRST REAL RUN OF THE NIGHTLY MODEL REFUSED TO MERGE, and it was right to. The orchestrator selected PR #181 as the single candidate, dispatched all four gates at its exact head with GITHUB_TOKEN, waited for 4/4 to complete, found project-governance FAILED, and stopped: verdict GATES_NOT_GREEN, exit 1, no merge. Every step of the sequence ran and the refusal came from the one condition that should produce it.

THE DEFECT IT FOUND was a THIRD validator encoding the retired trigger. tools/validate-branch-protection.py raised four FAILs -- each gate 'has no pull_request trigger, so its required context would never report on a PR and master would be permanently unmergeable'. The reasoning was correct and its premise had just been falsified by the very run reporting it: the context IS reported, by the dispatch, on the pull-request head. What that check really protects is that SOMETHING can report it, so it now requires the dispatch trigger.

That is the third place encoding 'must run on pull_request' -- project-state.py, validate-branch-protection.py -- and all three are resolved the same way: each keeps what it was actually protecting, and WHICH EVENT earns a required context is asserted in ONE place, against the model the register declares. A rule duplicated across three files is three chances to contradict yourself.

AND IT WAS FOUND BY THE MECHANISM, NOT BY READING. I had validated locally and all local validators passed, because validate-branch-protection.py needs the live GitHub API and is a gate step rather than part of preflight. The nightly model's first act was to catch a defect in its own activation.
an_obsolete_mutation_aborts_the_whole_su:
The second nightly run refused again, on M20: 'CI no longer runs on PRs to master', which replaced `pull_request:` in the governance workflow. That trigger is gone by decision, so the anchor did not resolve and run_mutations.py raised AssertionError('fixture drift') -- taking ALL 78 CASES with it.

THAT IS WORSE THAN THE EARLIER OBSOLETE CASES. M61, M61c and M61f failed for the wrong reason but still ran; a mutation whose anchor is missing raises BEFORE any assertion, so the matrix reports nothing at all about the 77 defects it does still cover. The suite goes from 'one case is wrong' to 'no case was checked'.

M20 is retargeted at the trigger that now earns the required context: disable the DISPATCH and the gate becomes unreachable and master permanently unmergeable, which is exactly what M20 always described.

AND THE GENERAL FIX RATHER THAN THE FOURTH SPECIFIC ONE: every `replace` anchor in all 78 cases is now audited against the tree, and there are zero stale. That audit is what should have been run the moment the delivery model changed -- four obsolete mutations in one mission is a pattern, not four coincidences.
